title: The enduring role of contracts for difference in risk management and market creation for renewables
venue: Nature Energy (Perspective), Vol. 9, pp. 20-26 (2024); published online Dec 2023. Authors: Beiter, Guillet, Jansen, Wilson, Kitzing.
claimSentence: "In this Perspective, we argue that the primary role of CfDs is risk management—rather than providing a subsidy—by creating a market for electricity supply at stable long-term prices." (Stated explicitly at the head of the roadmap paragraph; the title's word "enduring" pre-loads the secondary claim that CfDs are a lasting market feature, not a transitional crutch.)
openingMove: A three-step compression in the first two paragraphs. (1) A universal, slightly surprising fact that needs no citation-defense to feel true: "Electricity exchanged in competitive markets has high price volatility, unparalleled among traded commodities" — establishes the problem domain in one sentence. (2) Timeliness is bolted on immediately and concretely: "Russia's war on Ukraine has highlighted the sensitivity of electricity prices to gas supply shortages" — a recent, vivid event that makes price-shielding procurement urgent NOW. (3) The hook then narrows from the macro problem to the specific instrument and frames the misconception the paper will overturn: CfDs "have emerged as a favored procurement instrument," carry "more than 50% of future global supply" in offshore wind, yet "are sometimes labeled subsidy... which might imply for many that they support uneconomic activity." The opening thus moves problem -> why-now -> the wrong view it will correct, all before the thesis.
evidenceUse: Evidence is woven, not stacked, and almost every quantitative anchor is sourced to a numbered reference. The numbers are deployed as argumentative levers rather than decoration: (1) market-share anchor — ">50% of future global supply" via CfDs (establishes that the topic is non-niche); (2) the cost-structure spine — renewables have "around 80-90% of their lifetime costs as upfront fixed costs," with "very small O&M costs," vs fossil whose cost "is dominated by fuel expenses" (this single contrast carries the whole financing argument); (3) hedging-gap quantification — derivatives are "limited to a five-year period at most, with liquidity severely reduced for more than two years," against the "20-year (or more) financial lifetime" of the asset (the precise mismatch that motivates CfDs); (4) the subsidy-reframing numbers — "$447 billion per year" fossil subsidies vs "$128 billion" renewables subsidies, used to relativize and then dissolve the subsidy label. The authors lean heavily on their own prior published work (refs 31, 32 — Joule and Nature Energy) for the killer empirical claim that "offshore wind projects in mature markets are economically viable without subsidy payments ever paid out." Theory is also used as evidence: derivatives theory's "fair price" of a swap (expected net subsidy = zero) is the conceptual proof that a CfD need not be a subsidy.
counterargumentHandling: Unusually strong and structurally explicit for the genre — counterargument handling is the spine, not an afterthought. The entire paper is organized as a rebuttal of two named misconceptions ("the existence of CfDs is indicative of renewables being uneconomic" and "CfDs will become redundant over time and replaced by merchant operations"). Objections are stated in their strongest form before rebuttal: a dedicated section titled "CfDs are primarily about market creation and risk management, but are they also a subsidy?" concedes ground honestly — "We agree that CfDs could—particularly in a strictly legal sense—be considered a subsidy" and "CfDs have in the past certainly served governments' desire to convey a subsidy" — before pivoting on the functional-vs-legal distinction. The single-technology-auction objection is steel-manned both ways ("One could make the case that the resulting price difference constitutes a subsidy. On the other hand, one could argue..."). The downsides of the thesis are not hidden: "more limited value creation options for generators," CfDs "might hamper commercial forward markets," and the Simshauser quote that CfD-driven entry may be "poorly timed, poorly sized, poorly located." This balance is what makes it read as scholarship, not advocacy.
closingMove: A two-tier close. First a "Policy and future research implications" section that escalates the claim into the future — projecting CfD growth to "batteries, electrolyzers, and the transmission network," warning of market-distortion risks, and crucially naming SPECIFIC, non-generic research gaps: allocating price risk "among asset owners, ratepayers, and taxpayers" (noted as "largely absent from research"), and comparison against "alternative policy interventions, such as renewable portfolio standards or carbon pricing." Then a short explicit "To conclude" paragraph that restates the reframing as a research-community call to action: "we welcome more nuanced discussions on CfDs that focus on interdependencies with policy, risk management, market mechanisms, and the role of governments," tying back to economy-wide decarbonization. The outlook avoids the "more research is needed" failure mode by assigning concrete next questions to identifiable research streams (energy finance, market, policy) it earlier flagged as "fragmented."
figureUse: Three conceptual figures plus one table — all argument-legible, none raw-data plots. Figure 1 (two-panel a/b): capital-cost intensity of fossil vs solar PV vs wind, and the resulting merit-order/dispatch position — establishes the cost-structure premise visually. Figure 2 (a/b): wind vs gas cost-vs-spot-price over time, showing the wind asset entering "financial distress" when spot falls below fixed costs while gas income "floats above the debt service" — this figure IS the financing argument made visual, and its caption explicitly states the counter-intuitive payoff (distress "is independent of the comparative average costs"). Figure 3: a comparison schematic of price exposure and payment flows across CfD, PPA, mandated PPA, option contract, and merchant operation — the taxonomy figure that lets the prose make fine distinctions (e.g. one-sided CfD is "functionally closer to a financial option"). Table 1: a country-by-instrument matrix (UK, NL, DK, DE, FR, Taiwan, US-MA, US-MD, AUS-NSW) crossing duration, market sales, remuneration period, and curtailment treatment — the empirical breadth that backs "a variety of CfDs... has emerged." Figures are sourced ("adapted from ref. 19/31/32"), reinforcing the evidence-grounded posture. Each display item carries exactly one restatable message.
lengthRefsApprox: Main text approx 6,500 words in the accepted manuscript (the published Nature Energy version spans pp. 20-26, ~7 journal pages, likely trimmed toward ~5,000); 49 numbered references (heavy on energy-economics journals, policy consultation documents, and the authors' own prior work); 4 display items (3 conceptual figures + 1 table). Unstructured abstract of ~150 words with no references and no figure citations. No Key Points box. Standard back matter: Data availability, Acknowledgements, Author contributions, Declaration of interests.

sectionFlow.heading: Main (untitled introduction)
sectionFlow.move: Problem -> timeliness (Ukraine/gas) -> states the misconception (CfD=subsidy) -> delivers the thesis and a three-part roadmap ('First... Second... Third...') that previews the reframing, the de-risking payoff, and the call to integrate fragmented research.

sectionFlow.heading: A long-term price hedge is needed for renewables financing
sectionFlow.move: Establishes the causal premise: renewables are 80-90% upfront-fixed-cost and price-takers, so merchant exposure to volatile spot prices creates default risk lenders won't bear; existing hedges (forwards, CPPAs) are too short and too thin, leaving a hedging gap a CfD must fill. This is the 'why the instrument is necessary' foundation.

sectionFlow.heading: CfDs primarily manage price risk and are less about a subsidy (with sub-headed parts: 'A variety of CfD types exist...', 'Mutual benefits...', 'CfDs are primarily about market creation... but are they also a subsidy?')
sectionFlow.move: Defines the instrument mechanically (floating-for-fixed swap), surveys design variants and counterparties (who bears risk: ratepayers vs taxpayers), shows the deal is mutually beneficial at signing, then confronts the subsidy label head-on using the legal-vs-functional distinction and derivatives 'fair price' theory to argue expected net subsidy can be zero.

sectionFlow.heading: Policy and future research implications of CfD growth
sectionFlow.move: Escalates the claim forward in time (CfDs spread to batteries, electrolyzers, grid), acknowledges systemic risks (distorted entry signals, weakened forward markets), and converts the thesis into a concrete, multi-disciplinary research agenda on risk allocation among owners/ratepayers/taxpayers.

sectionFlow.heading: To conclude (closing paragraph)
sectionFlow.move: Restates the reframing as a community call for 'more nuanced discussions' and ties CfD risk-allocation understanding to enabling economy-wide decarbonization.

transferableLessons: Put your reframing in the title via one load-bearing adjective. 'Enduring' silently asserts the whole thesis (CfDs are permanent, not transitional). For the AI-compute piece, a title like 'Exporting stranded clean electricity as compute, not electrons' front-loads the claim and the contrast in <12 words.

Hook with a recent, concrete event to manufacture timeliness in sentence 3-4. They used Russia/Ukraine gas shocks. Your equivalent: the 2024-2026 datacenter electricity-demand surge and grid-interconnection queues / curtailment of renewables — name a specific number and a specific year so a reviewer cannot say 'this could have been written five years ago.'

State the misconception you overturn BEFORE your thesis, then deliver the thesis in one first-person sentence ('In this Perspective, we argue that...'). Your misconception to name: 'stranded renewables are a transmission problem to be solved with more wires.' Your thesis: ship the value as tokens over fiber, not electrons over lines.

Use a numbered 'First... Second... Third...' roadmap paragraph at the end of the intro. It pre-sells each body section and tells reviewers exactly what you will and won't argue. Map yours to: (1) the physical/economic case (compute co-located with stranded generation beats transmission), (2) the feasibility/precedent case, (3) the research-and-policy agenda.

Build the whole argument on ONE quantitative contrast and make it a figure. Theirs was the 80-90%-fixed-cost vs fuel-dominated-cost structure, visualized in Fig 1-2. Yours should be a single back-of-envelope cost-crossover figure: $/MWh transmitted-and-curtailed-electron value vs $/MWh converted-to-tokens value (including transmission losses, interconnection delay, and curtailment avoided). One restatable message per figure.

Relativize-then-dissolve the framing you reject using a big comparison number, exactly as they did with $447B fossil vs $128B renewable subsidies. For you: contrast the capital and years to build long-distance transmission against the capital and months to stand up datacenter compute at the resource — make the conventional 'export electrons' path look slow and expensive by comparison.

Lean on your own and others' published empirical results for the one killer claim, with a DOI. They cited their Joule and Nature Energy papers to assert 'viable without subsidy ever paid out.' Find the strongest published number on curtailment volumes, datacenter PUE/efficiency, or token-energy intensity and let it carry your central feasibility claim.

Devote a real, honestly-titled section to your strongest counterargument, conceding the legitimate part first. They wrote '...but are they also a subsidy?' and granted 'we agree that... in a strictly legal sense.' Yours: 'But isn't compute export just stranding the value differently?' — concede latency-sensitive and sovereignty concerns, then rebut on the economics. Steel-man both sides ('One could argue... On the other hand...').

Generalize the claim at the end to make it feel inevitable, then escalate to a research agenda. They extended CfDs to batteries/electrolyzers/grid. You can extend 'value-not-electrons export' to other stranded resources (flared gas already does this informally, remote hydro, desert solar) — framing your idea as one instance of a broader principle.

Close by naming SPECIFIC, currently-absent research questions and assigning them to identifiable communities, not 'more research is needed.' They named risk-allocation among owners/ratepayers/taxpayers and comparison to RPS/carbon pricing. Yours: name the missing accounting framework (how to credit a region for embedded-energy exports), the grid-vs-fiber siting optimization, and the carbon-accounting attribution problem — and call on energy-systems, ML-systems, and trade-policy researchers to integrate.

Keep authorial 'we' for claim-bearing moments only and calibrate speculation explicitly. Match their move of separating established fact ('80-90% upfront'), reasoned inference ('this implies lenders focus on the lowest price'), and forward conjecture ('CfDs might become essential to future market design'). Reviewers forgive bold claims that are visibly flagged as forward-looking.

Target the house spec: ~4,000-5,000 words, unstructured ~150-200-word abstract with no refs or figure cites, 3-5 headed argument-ordered (not topic-ordered) sections, ~30-100 references skewed toward primary sources plus recent policy documents, and 2-5 conceptual display items. Pull 5-8 recent natenergy Perspectives to confirm current house structure before drafting.

title: Policy credibility is a key component for an effective and efficient EU Emissions Trading System
venue: Nature Energy (vol. 9, pp. 637–638, published 18 June 2024). NOTE: the article carries the type label "Policy Brief," NOT "Perspective." It is a ~2-page front-matter companion to a full research article (Bocklet/Pahle et al. style; the linked primary paper is "EU carbon prices signal high policy credibility and farsighted actors", s41560-024-01505-x). Treat its craft as that of a tightly compressed argument-brief, and scale its moves up when writing a true 4,000–5,000-word Perspective.
claimSentence: "Recent reforms of the EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) boosted carbon prices by tightening the cap on emission allowances and increasing political commitment to it, which effectively made actors more farsighted. Policymakers should thus view prices as an indicator of credibility as well as scarcity, and manage potential future drops in the former by renewing commitment to the cap." (The reframing is the single load-bearing move: price = scarcity signal AND credibility signal.)

sectionFlow.heading: (Untitled lead paragraph / abstract-as-lead)
sectionFlow.move: States the whole argument in two sentences before any evidence: what happened (reforms raised prices), the mechanism (commitment made actors farsighted), and the prescriptive takeaway (read prices as credibility, defend that credibility). A Policy Brief front-loads its conclusion.

sectionFlow.heading: Body narrative (unheaded)
sectionFlow.move: Walks the causal chain: cap tightening + political commitment -> credibility -> actor foresight -> efficient price level (~€80/tCO2). Establishes the conventional framing (price = scarcity) and substitutes the reframing (price ALSO = credibility) as the new lens.

sectionFlow.heading: Figure 1 — 'Impact of reforms and actors' foresight on carbon prices'
sectionFlow.move: The single display item does the quantitative heavy lifting: visualizes how reforms + foresight (high vs low credibility) map to price trajectories, making the ~3x differential legible at a glance. One figure, one message.

sectionFlow.heading: Messages for policy (the only labelled section; 4 bullets)
sectionFlow.move: Converts the analysis into 4 escalating policy claims: (1) low credibility -> only short-term cap met -> stranded assets; (2) the two reforms instilled credibility -> ~€80 price consistent with dynamic cost-effectiveness; (3) the credibility price effect is large (~3x); (4) policymakers must sustain credibility and intervene if prices signal it has dropped. This is the brief's argumentative spine.

sectionFlow.heading: Further reading
sectionFlow.move: Replaces a full reference list with 4 curated pointers (Dolphin et al.; Quemin & Trotignon; Pahle et al.; Brunner et al.) — signalling lineage and where to verify the evidence, not exhaustively citing it.

openingMove: Opens cold with the finding itself rather than a scene or statistic: "Recent reforms of the EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) boosted carbon prices by tightening the cap... and increasing political commitment to it, which effectively made actors more farsighted." Timeliness is implicit and structural — it anchors to two named, recent EU ETS reforms and the observed price run-up (from <€10/tCO2 in 2017 to ~€80/tCO2 in 2022, a ~10x rise the companion paper documents), so 'why now' = a fresh, dramatic price crossover that demanded a causal explanation. The hook is the surprising reattribution: the price spike was not just scarcity, it was credibility.
evidenceUse: Lean and anchor-driven, not survey-driven. Three numbers carry the entire piece: (1) the target/observed efficient price ~€80 per tCO2; (2) the headline contrast that a farsighted (high-credibility) market sits ~3x above a short-sighted (low-credibility) market in near-term prices — a single ratio that makes the abstract concept 'credibility' quantitatively tangible; (3) the backdrop ~10x price rise over five years (and EU ETS ~40% of EU GHG, from the press framing). Crucially the numbers are tied to a model result ('consistent with what model results suggest is dynamically cost-effective'), so the brief leans on the companion research article for derivation rather than re-deriving anything. Evidence is marshalled to convert a qualitative claim (credibility matters) into a falsifiable quantity (a ~3x price wedge).
counterargumentHandling: Minimal and implicit, as the compressed genre allows. The strongest objection — that the price rise is just scarcity (cap tightening) and credibility is an unnecessary add-on — is not given a dedicated section; instead it is pre-empted by the framing 'credibility as well as scarcity' (additive, not either/or), which concedes scarcity is real while arguing it is incomplete. The downside risk is acknowledged in bullet 4 (prices could 'drop again to levels that signal low credibility'), which doubles as a falsification condition and a hedge. A full Perspective would owe a much fuller treatment here; the brief gets away with a one-clause concession.
closingMove: Ends on a forward-looking, prescriptive note rather than a summary: bullet 4 instructs policymakers to 'take precautions to sustain high credibility and consider suitable interventions if prices drop again to levels that signal low credibility.' The future direction is concrete and actor-specific (policymakers, named intervention trigger = a price drop), not the generic 'more research is needed.' It closes the loop opened by the lead — having argued price=credibility, the payoff is an actionable monitoring rule.
figureUse: Exactly one figure (Figure 1, 'Impact of reforms and actors' foresight on carbon prices') and no tables or boxes. It is a conceptual/quantitative figure that contrasts price trajectories under high- vs low-credibility (farsighted vs short-sighted) actor assumptions across the reform events — i.e., it visualizes the ~3x wedge and the mechanism in one panel. The figure carries the one message a reader could restate in a sentence; the prose does not duplicate it but points to it.
lengthRefsApprox: Very short: ~2 printed pages (637–638), roughly 700–1,100 words of main text — characteristic of the Nature Energy 'Policy Brief' format, NOT the 4,000–5,000-word Perspective. 1 display item (Figure 1); 0 boxes/tables. References are handled as a curated 'Further reading' list of ~4 items rather than a full citation apparatus (a full Perspective would carry 60–100). One labelled section ('Messages for policy', 4 bullets) plus lead, figure, and further reading.
transferableLessons: Lead with the reframing, not the topic. This brief's whole force comes from one substitution — 'price is a credibility signal as well as a scarcity signal.' For the AI-compute piece, pin an equivalent one-sentence reframing up front: 'Stranded clean electricity should be exported as tokens over fiber, not electrons over wires.' Everything else defends that sentence.

Make the abstract IS the thesis. The opening two sentences state mechanism + prescription before any evidence. Open your Perspective the same way: in two sentences say what changed (cheap stranded renewables + cheap inference), the mechanism (compute co-locates with energy; tokens ship at near-zero marginal transmission cost), and the prescription (build compute at the stranded resource).

Convert the abstract concept into ONE killer ratio. 'Credibility' became real the moment it was '~3x higher near-term prices.' Find your single comparable anchor — e.g. 'exporting a stranded MWh as AI tokens captures Nx the delivered value of exporting it as electrons after transmission losses + curtailment,' and make that ratio the spine of a figure.

Earn timeliness from a recent crossover, not from rhetoric. The brief implicitly leans on the 2017->2022 ~10x price run-up. Anchor yours to a dated, recent crossover: the post-2023 collapse in inference cost per token, GPU/datacenter siting announcements at stranded hydro/solar, and curtailment statistics from a named recent year.

One figure, one restatable message. The brief spends its single display item on the mechanism contrast (high vs low credibility trajectories). Budget your figures the same way — e.g. one 'value-per-stranded-MWh: electrons vs tokens' crossover chart, one 'token export pathway' schematic — and let prose point to them rather than reprint them.

Pre-empt the strongest objection by making the claim additive, not exclusionary. 'Credibility AS WELL AS scarcity' disarms the 'it's just scarcity' rebuttal. For you, frame tokens as complement-then-substitute to transmission ('where new lines are slow or stranded capacity is structural'), conceding transmission's role rather than denying it — but in a TRUE Perspective give this its own honest counterargument section (latency-sensitive vs batch workloads, water/cooling, grid-services value of electrons, jurisdictional/data-sovereignty risk).

Close with an actionable monitoring rule, not a platitude. The brief ends with a falsifiable trigger ('intervene if prices drop'). End yours with concrete, actor-specific next steps and a falsification condition — e.g. 'site batch-inference clusters at curtailment hotspots; revisit if delivered-token value falls below firmed-transmission value,' naming who acts (developers, grid operators, regulators).

Mind the GENRE GAP when reusing this template. This is a ~700-1,100-word Policy Brief with 4 'Messages for policy' and a 'Further reading' list. A Nature Energy Perspective is 4-10x longer with 3-5 headed body sections, 60-100 references, 2-5 display items, and a dedicated counterargument section. Reuse this brief's compression and reframing discipline, but scaffold a full evidence spine and an honest limits section to meet the Perspective spec.

Carry the prescription in numbered, escalating 'messages.' Even in a long Perspective, the brief's 4-bullet escalation (failure mode -> what worked -> magnitude -> what to do) is a clean Key-Points-box template. Draft your 4-6 Key Points first as the argument's skeleton, then expand each into a body section.

title: The expansion of natural gas infrastructure puts energy transitions at risk
venue: Nature Energy 7, 582-587 (2022) — Perspective. Authors: Kemfert, Präger, Braunger, Hoffart, Brauers (DIW Berlin et al.). DOI: 10.1038/s41560-022-01060-3
claimSentence: "In this Perspective, we argue why the expansion of natural gas infrastructure hinders a renewable energy future and why the natural gas 'bridge' narrative is misleading" — i.e., gas is not a bridge technology; its underestimated methane/climate impact, plus carbon lock-in and stranded-asset risk, mean expansion actively delays decarbonisation rather than enabling it.

sectionFlow.heading: Abstract (unstructured, ~160 words, no refs/figures)
sectionFlow.move: States the controversy, then immediately announces the device: 'we combine five perspectives to argue why...'. Compresses the thesis (gas is no bridge) and pre-lists the five recommendations, so the reader knows the payload before reading.

sectionFlow.heading: Introduction (no subheading)
sectionFlow.move: Background + timeliness + claim + roadmap in four moves. Establishes that gas is still expanding, anchors urgency to the 2022 Russia-Ukraine war and the EU/German LNG buildout, then pivots ('questions now arise as to whether a rapid decline... might be necessary, instead of expansion') and states the claim plus a roadmap sentence naming the five arguments.

sectionFlow.heading: 1. Methane emissions are much higher than previously estimated
sectionFlow.move: Climate-science sub-claim. Attacks the factual premise of the pro-gas case (gas as clean coal-substitute) by marshalling leakage and GWP numbers, undermining the foundation all later sections rest on.

sectionFlow.heading: 2. Emissions from natural gas are poorly treated in scenarios
sectionFlow.move: Methodological sub-claim. Argues the models that justify gas use bake in outdated assumptions (old GWP100, ignored leakage), so the evidence base proponents cite is itself biased; widens to hydrogen/blue-hydrogen leakage and 100%-renewable feasibility.

sectionFlow.heading: 3. Misleading narratives prevent a direct shift to renewables
sectionFlow.move: Discursive sub-claim and the dedicated counterargument engagement. Reconstructs the 'bridge technology'/'transition fuel' narrative in its strongest, most coherent form, then dismantles it by showing it migrated from coal (1970s) to gas (post-2008 shale) and is strategically vague about endpoint and end-date.

sectionFlow.heading: 4. Natural gas lock-ins delay renewable energy transitions
sectionFlow.move: Infrastructural/institutional sub-claim. Shows decades-long asset lifetimes create carbon lock-in; uses the committed-emissions number to prove existing infrastructure already busts the 1.5C budget, and rebuts the 'repurpose for hydrogen/e-fuels' escape hatch.

sectionFlow.heading: 5. Investments in gas infrastructure imply economic risks
sectionFlow.move: Economic sub-claim and the strongest pragmatic case. Reframes gas not as cheap-and-safe but as financially dangerous via stranded assets, capital misallocation, and systemic financial-sector contagion; lands the largest dollar figures here.

sectionFlow.heading: Outlook (no subheading)
sectionFlow.move: One-sentence synthesis of the whole indictment, then converts the five diagnostic sections 1:1 into five prescriptive, actor-directed recommendations, closing on the inevitability framing ('inevitably implies a fossil natural gas exit').

openingMove: Opens not with the thesis but with a tension: gas use 'experienced steep growth' and is being justified as a transition aid, immediately followed by hard expansion numbers (~500 GW of planned/under-construction gas plants; 635 Mt/yr LNG import and 700 Mt/yr export terminals). Timeliness is bolted on explicitly and contemporaneously: 'a new geopolitical order has been created after Russia entered war with Ukraine,' EU 40%+ Russian-gas dependence, and Germany's draft law for up to 11 LNG terminals importing gas 'until 2043.' The hook is the collision between a real, accelerating, multi-decade buildout and climate goals — making 'now' the moment to challenge it before the concrete is poured.
evidenceUse: Dense, ranged, and always sourced — a model of 'argue from existing published evidence.' Quantitative anchors are stacked: fossil fuels = 15-22% of methane emissions; anthropogenic fossil methane underestimated by 20-60% (regionally 50-60% in US/Canada); the gas-vs-coal advantage vanishes above ~3.2-3.4% leakage while global average is ~2.2% but individual fields hit 6% and up to 17%; superemitters = ~1/3 of shale-site emissions; methane GWP up to 87x CO2 over 20 years and 36x over 100 years. Lock-in and economics get the biggest numbers: existing infrastructure commits ~658 Gt CO2 vs a 420-580 Gt 1.5C budget; stranded fossil assets = USD 7-11 trillion; USD 2.3 trillion of gas/oil projects misaligned with Paris; up to USD 90 billion stranded by 2030 (USD 400 billion by 2050). Crucially, almost every number is given as a range with the primary source named, and uncertainty is flagged honestly ('estimates on global gas infrastructure stranding are not yet available').
counterargumentHandling: Exemplary and central, not bolted-on. The piece is organized as a serial rebuttal: each body section opens by stating the pro-gas argument in its strongest form ('It is often argued that...', 'Another argument that proponents of natural gas use is...', 'often described as a climate-friendly alternative') before demolishing it. Section 3 is a fully dedicated counterargument section that takes the opposing 'bridge technology' narrative seriously as a rhetorically coherent story ('seems coherent as long as it is convincing...') and then exposes why it is coherent yet wrong — its strategic vagueness and its suspicious portability from coal to gas. The authors also concede partial ground honestly ('natural gas might help with the last few percent of energy provision') and acknowledge gaps in their own side's evidence base, which raises credibility.
closingMove: A two-tier close. First a single periodic synthesis sentence that restacks the whole indictment ('a fossil fuel with a high climate impact, often hidden under a misleading narrative, which hinders decarbonisation... cannot be a solution'). Then a structured, non-generic outlook: five numbered recommendations that map exactly onto the five body sections (First... manage methane; Second... revise scenarios; Third... replace narratives with unambiguous criteria; Fourth... avoid further lock-ins; Fifth... take asset-stranding risk seriously), each addressed to specific actors (modellers, policymakers, private and state investors). It ends on a forward, quasi-deterministic note — Paris compliance 'inevitably implies a fossil natural gas exit,' and the earlier it is planned, the more budget remains for hard-to-abate sectors — converting critique into a call to action.
figureUse: Notably, the accepted manuscript contains and cites zero figures, boxes, or tables — there are no 'Fig. 1' callouts anywhere in the body. The argument is carried entirely by prose and embedded numbers, with the 'five perspectives' framing itself serving as the organizing device a figure would normally provide. This is a deliberate, viable structural choice for a heavily quantitative, argument-dense Perspective: the section scaffold does the work of a conceptual figure. (The published Nature Energy version may carry at most one editor-added conceptual graphic, but the article does not depend on it.)
lengthRefsApprox: ~4,800-5,200 words of main text across 6 published pages (Nature Energy 7, 582-587); 91 references; 0 figures, 0 boxes, 0 tables cited in the manuscript body. Reference density is high (~18-19 refs per 1,000 words), heavy on primary Nature-family and energy-policy literature, reflecting that the whole case is built by re-weighting published evidence.
transferableLessons: Use a numbered multi-lens scaffold as your spine. Their 'five perspectives' (climate-science, methodological, discursive, infrastructural, economic) is reusable verbatim: argue 'stranded clean electricity should be exported as AI tokens, not electrons' through five lenses — physics/loss economics, grid-modelling assumptions, the 'just build more transmission' narrative, infrastructure lock-in, and capital/stranded-asset risk.

Make every section a rebuttal, not a survey. Open each body section by stating the conventional case in its strongest form ('It is often argued that surplus power is best moved by HVDC lines...') and then dismantle it. This structure forces you to engage objections continuously rather than quarantining them.

Bolt timeliness to a dated, concrete, current event. They anchored to the 2022 war and specific LNG bills with end-years. For the AI-compute piece, anchor to a 2025-2026 datacentre-buildout/curtailment crossover, a named grid-interconnection backlog, or a specific 'powering AI' announcement, with figures and a year.

Lead with the factual premise-buster. Their strongest move is destroying the 'gas is clean' premise (methane/GWP numbers) before anything else. Your equivalent: first dismantle the assumption that electrons are the cheapest export of stranded power — quantify transmission losses, interconnection queues, and curtailment rates versus the marginal cost of moving a token over fiber.

Quantify with sourced ranges and the crossover number. Their decisive figure is the 658 Gt vs 420-580 Gt budget collision and the multi-trillion stranded-asset totals. Find your single killer comparison (e.g. USD/MWh delivered as electrons after losses+wheeling vs USD-equivalent value of the same MWh converted to inference tokens) and present it as a range with primary sources, flagging where data is missing.

Reframe the asset you defend as the safer bet against stranding. They turned gas from 'cheap/reliable' into 'financially dangerous (stranded assets).' Mirror it: frame transmission megaprojects as the lock-in/stranding risk and modular compute-export as the flexible, de-riskable alternative.

Convert your diagnosis into actor-directed recommendations that map 1:1 to your sections. Avoid 'more research is needed.' End with N numbered recommendations each naming who must act (grid planners, ISOs, datacentre operators, financiers) — exactly mirroring your N body sections, as they did.

Concede the limit honestly to buy credibility. They admit gas may cover 'the last few percent' and that stranding data is incomplete. Concede where electrons still win (local load, latency-sensitive uses) so the token-export claim reads as scholarship, not advocacy.

You can run a Perspective with no figures if the section scaffold is the argument — but in Nature Energy a single conceptual crossover/decision figure (cost-per-delivered-value of electrons vs tokens) would strengthen an inherently quantitative claim; plan one per major sub-claim.

Budget ~4,500-5,000 words and 60-90 references of mostly primary, recent, Nature-family literature; carry a DOI for every quantitative anchor and verify each number against its primary source before submission.

title: Rapid fuel switching from coal to natural gas through effective carbon pricing
venue: Nature Energy, vol. 3, pp. 365-372 (2018). Article type: Perspective. Authors: Grant Wilson (Univ. Sheffield) and Iain Staffell (Imperial College London). DOI 10.1038/s41560-018-0109-0.
claimSentence: "This Perspective argues that with the right conditions, both in terms of pre-existing infrastructure and political will, switching away from coal has an important role to play in the rapid early decarbonisation of power systems." Operationalised in the abstract as: with the right incentives (notably a strong, stable carbon price), power-sector fuel switching could achieve ~1 GtCO2/yr savings worldwide (~3% of global emissions), "buying precious time to slow the growth in cumulative carbon emissions." The thesis is a single mechanism (carbon price unlocking idle gas capacity) generalised from one proof case (Britain) to a global estimate.

sectionFlow.heading: Abstract (unlabelled, structured)
sectionFlow.move: Compresses the whole argument into one arc: a surprising fact (Britain's emissions fell 6% in 2016), a reframing (not renewables/nuclear but 'much-overlooked' coal-to-gas switching), the question (enabling conditions + global potential), the finding (spare capacity must pre-exist; political will/carbon price is the bigger lever), and the quantified stakes (~1 GtCO2/yr, 3% of global). Front-loads the payoff before any evidence.

sectionFlow.heading: Introduction (unlabelled lead)
sectionFlow.move: Establishes timeliness and a gap. Opens on rising global emissions (37 GtCO2/yr, +2.4%/yr), notes fuel switching is recognised for transport but 'lacks such recognition' in the power sector. Pre-empts the obvious alternatives (renewables only 5% of global generation; CCS may need three decades for a 10% share) to argue why a months-not-decades option deserves attention. Honestly concedes upfront that gas is not a long-term fix (~0.4x coal emissions; +25% if shale). Pivots to Britain as the living proof, then plants the explicit thesis sentence after Figure 1.

sectionFlow.heading: Britain's power generation
sectionFlow.move: Builds the proof case with history and magnitude. Traces the 1990s 'dash-for-gas' (coal share 66%->34% over 1991-99), then the recent collapse (coal 75%->9% in four years; power emissions 158->78 MtCO2). Isolates the causal claim: in 2015-16 the coal fall was filled 'entirely by natural gas' (coal -46 TWh, gas +43 TWh, renewables <1 TWh) — a clean attribution that rules out the renewables explanation.

sectionFlow.heading: Britain's commitment to reduce coal power
sectionFlow.move: Adds policy and narrative context, framing Britain as a world-first (2025 unabated-coal phase-out; Powering Past Coal Alliance). Uses a striking asymmetry — 14 years to ramp coal demand up (1936-50) vs 1 year to reverse it (2015-16) — to dramatise that rapid change is possible. Notes enabling pre-conditions (80% of fleet >30 years old, pollution directives).

sectionFlow.heading: Factors that enabled Britain's rapid fuel switch
sectionFlow.move: Distils the mechanism into a reusable four-factor checklist: (1) pre-built spare gas capacity, (2) fuel supply infrastructure that can cope, (3) political will / effective carbon price, (4) fuel prices close enough to avoid large consumer price rises. This is the analytical core that makes the case transferable rather than anecdotal, and sets up the country comparisons.

sectionFlow.heading: Putting a price on carbon
sectionFlow.move: Argues the central causal lever. States the authors' view that the carbon price (Carbon Price Support/Floor, 2013) was the primary driver, contrasting the weak EU-ETS (~5/tCO2) with the UK floor (18/tCO2). Quantifies the modest cost (~0.7 p/kWh, ~5% of retail) against the large benefit (~25% emissions cut), and concedes the policy's limits (regulatory risk, frozen rate, failure to spur new low-carbon build).

sectionFlow.heading: Leaving the markets to it
sectionFlow.move: Comparative case 1 (US): shows the mechanism can run on market forces alone (shale-driven gas prices -70% since 2005), but slower and politically fragile (Trump-era reversals). Draws the policy lesson that long-term legal targets (UK 2008 Climate Change Act) outperform shifting federal regulation — strengthening the carbon-price/political-will thesis by contrast.

sectionFlow.heading: Potential for fuel switching in Germany
sectionFlow.move: Comparative case 2 (Germany): the instructive counter-example. A renewables 'champion' that decarbonised little (-15% vs Britain's -61%) because it kept lignite/hard coal and lacked a carbon-price signal. Shows latent potential (24 GW idle gas at 18% utilisation could cut ~62 MtCO2/yr) while honestly cataloguing why it hasn't happened (import dependency, nuclear exit, lignite lobby) — demonstrating the four factors by their partial absence.

sectionFlow.heading: Potential for fuel switching globally
sectionFlow.move: Scales the claim from anecdote to global number. Spells out the order-of-magnitude method (30 largest coal nations = 97% of capacity; CCGT at 80%, OCGT 0-40% utilisation; defined carbon intensities) before giving results, so the headline figure feels earned. Result: 0.8-1.2 GtCO2/yr, ~3% of global; with country texture (US/Russia 40-50% convertible; China/India only 6-12%).

sectionFlow.heading: No Silver Bullet
sectionFlow.move: The dedicated counterargument section — the integrity move. Explicitly hedges ('first-order approximation') and lists barriers: energy-security/import-dependency shifts, coal-community employment and political opposition, carbon leakage/'offshoring' (Britain importing high-carbon Dutch power), methane leakage, and that carbon pricing fails where gas infrastructure is absent (Poland, Japan). Concedes switching is reversible. This inoculates the thesis against the obvious rebuttals.

sectionFlow.heading: Conclusions
sectionFlow.move: Restates the thesis with its boundary condition ('temporary stepping stone', incompatible with deep decarbonisation absent CCS) and reasserts the 'quick win' framing. Reprises Britain's headline numbers and a head-to-head speed comparison (fuel switch saved 25 MtCO2 in 1 year vs renewables' 22 MtCO2 over 6 years vs ~10 years for new nuclear). Closes on the cumulative-emissions stakes and a rhetorical call ('it is about time...benefits...received greater attention').

sectionFlow.heading: Methods + References
sectionFlow.move: Methods makes the global estimate auditable (four-stage calculation, data sources Platts/Enerdata/IEA/Bloomberg, three explicit simplifying caveats, worked Japan/Britain/US examples, data-availability via Figshare). 87 references and 3 supplementary tables anchor a opinion-led genre in verifiable data.

openingMove: The lead sentence is a counterintuitive, concrete statistic that doubles as a hook and a timeliness marker: Britain's overall carbon emissions fell 6% in 2016 from cleaner electricity. The very next sentences perform a reframing/myth-bust — 'This was not due to a surge in low-carbon nuclear or renewable sources; instead it was the much-overlooked impact of fuel switching from coal to natural gas.' Timeliness is then reinforced in the Introduction by anchoring to fresh global numbers (37 GtCO2/yr, emissions stabilised 2014-16 then rising again) and current policy moments (COP21, the 2025 coal phase-out). The hook formula = a surprising recent fact + 'everyone is looking at the wrong cause' + 'this deserves attention now.'
evidenceUse: Evidence is dense, specific, and always sourced (87 refs for a ~3,500-word body). Numbers do rhetorical work in three modes: (1) attribution numbers that isolate causation (coal -46 TWh, gas +43 TWh, renewables <1 TWh in 2015-16 — proving gas not renewables filled the gap); (2) magnitude/speed numbers dramatising the change (coal share 75%->9% in 4 years; 14 years up vs 1 year down; British switch in 2016 exceeded all other European countries combined); (3) cost-benefit framing that pre-empts the affordability objection (carbon floor added ~0.7 p/kWh, ~5%, yet facilitated ~25% emissions cut). The global headline (~1 GtCO2/yr) is presented as an explicit range (0.8-1.2 Gt; 13-27% of coal) with a sensitivity figure, signalling honesty about uncertainty. Authorial judgement is openly flagged ('Our view is that...', 'It is our view that...') rather than hidden, which is genre-appropriate for a Perspective.
counterargumentHandling: Strong and structurally privileged. Objections are handled in two ways: (a) distributed concessions throughout (gas is ~0.4x coal but still high-carbon and incompatible with deep decarbonisation; the carbon floor failed to spur new low-carbon build; switching is reversible; the global estimate is only first-order); and (b) a dedicated section titled 'No Silver Bullet' that names and engages the main rebuttals — energy security/import dependency, coal-mining communities and political opposition, carbon leakage/'offshoring', methane leakage, and the policy's uselessness where gas infrastructure is absent. The Germany case functions as a built-in counter-example (renewables leadership without decarbonisation), and Methods lists three explicit simplifying caveats. The effect is that the thesis is bounded ('temporary stepping stone') rather than overclaimed, which makes the central claim more credible.
closingMove: Two-paragraph close. First it re-scopes the claim defensively (fuel switching 'can only ever be a temporary stepping stone'; gains must not be 'squandered by the extended use of gas' as a substitute for low-carbon build) and connects to a higher stake (cumulative emissions; easing the burden on future generations facing negative emissions). Then it ends on a punchy, almost editorial call to action: 'The potential for rapid and material global emissions reductions appears to have gone unnoticed thus far; it is about time that the benefits of fuel switching received greater attention.' Future directions are seeded earlier and explicitly: a 'detailed country-by-country analysis...will be a valuable area of future work', and 'Recreating this analysis using open-access data is a logical and important next step.'
figureUse: Six numbered figures, all data/empirical (no conceptual schematic, no boxes, no in-text tables; 3 supplementary tables sit in Methods). Each figure is load-bearing and tied to a specific argumentative beat: Fig 1 (carbon intensity of 6 countries over 50 years) sets the comparative benchmark and quantifies 'how fast is fast' via a legend of depth/duration of cuts; Fig 2 (generation mix, GB/DE/US, 25 yr) supplies the attribution evidence; Fig 3 (British coal mined vs burned since 1850) delivers the historical-reversal drama; Fig 4 (wholesale price vs fuel+carbon cost benchmark, two panels with/without carbon price) is the causal mechanism made visible; Fig 5 (DE vs GB emissions with carbon price overlaid) is the natural experiment showing the price as the differentiator; Fig 6 (two-panel scatter of 30 countries + sensitivity of the GtCO2 estimate) carries the global generalisation. Captions are unusually full — they state the takeaway, the method, and the data sources, so each figure is self-contained.
lengthRefsApprox: Main text ~3,500-3,800 words (abstract ~140 words; body+captions ~4,400 word-tokens). 6 main figures; 0 boxes; 0 in-text tables; 3 supplementary tables. 87 numbered references. Methods section ~1,500 words. Two authors. AAM is 25 pages including refs.
transferableLessons: Open with a counterintuitive, verifiable statistic that reframes the reader's mental model, then immediately name the misconception you are correcting. For the AI-compute piece: lead with a concrete stranded-energy number (e.g. 'X TWh/yr of curtailed wind and solar was thrown away in 2025') and the reframe: the bottleneck on exporting that value is not transmission lines or batteries but that we keep trying to move electrons instead of moving the tokens those electrons could compute.

State the central claim explicitly in one sentence early (Wilson & Staffell put it right after Figure 1) and again in the abstract with a single quantified headline. Your equivalent of '~1 GtCO2/yr (3% of global)' should be one defensible top-line number — e.g. inference tokens or economic value per stranded TWh, or CO2 displaced per exported token — derived transparently so reviewers can check it.

Distil your thesis into a small, reusable checklist of enabling conditions, as they did with four factors. For compute-export, propose your own 3-5 (e.g. cheap stranded/curtailed power; latency-tolerant or batchable AI workloads; siteable datacentre + cooling; cross-border data/compute market and pricing signal; policy that values exported compute like exported electricity). The checklist is what makes the argument portable to other countries and gives the paper its analytical spine.

Argue from a proof case, then scale to a global estimate via a clearly-stated order-of-magnitude method. They used Britain -> 30 countries. You could anchor on one real instance (a hyperscaler or crypto-to-AI site co-located with stranded renewables) and then estimate global stranded-clean-TWh that is latency-tolerant, with an explicit utilisation/conversion assumption (TWh -> tokens or compute-hours -> exportable value) and a sensitivity range, mirroring their 0.8-1.2 Gt band.

Use comparison cases to demonstrate the mechanism by both presence and absence. They contrasted market-driven US, policy-driven Britain, and stalled Germany. You can contrast a region exporting electrons via interconnectors/HVDC (lossy, congested, slow to permit) vs a region 'exporting' the same energy as compute (datacentre + fibre), and a cautionary case where compute export failed because a precondition (fibre, water, or market rules) was missing.

Make the cost/benefit framing explicit and pre-empt the affordability/efficiency objection with a small ratio, as they did with 0.7 p/kWh -> 25% emissions cut. For AI compute, quantify value-per-MWh or jobs/GDP-per-exported-TWh of compute versus the marginal value of the same TWh shipped as electrons or curtailed to zero.

Devote a named section to honest counterarguments ('No Silver Bullet' is a memorable, disarming heading). Yours should engage: transmission/interconnection alternatives and when electrons still win, water and local-grid strain, carbon intensity if the 'stranded' power is not truly additional, data sovereignty and security, jobs/equity in exporting regions, and the rebound risk that cheap compute simply induces more demand. Bound your claim ('a complement, not a replacement, for grid build-out').

Engineer the figures to each carry one argumentative beat and write self-contained captions stating the takeaway, method and sources. Plan ~6 data figures: a benchmark figure (stranded/curtailed energy trends across regions), an attribution figure, a cost/mechanism figure, a natural-experiment comparison, and a two-panel global-potential scatter + sensitivity analysis. A single conceptual schematic (electrons-vs-tokens export pathway) is acceptable but keep most figures empirical, as Nature Energy expects.

Close by re-scoping defensively then issuing a forward call, and seed concrete future-work hooks (they flagged 'country-by-country analysis' and 'open-access data'). End with an editorial line that names the overlooked opportunity, and propose specific next steps (standardised compute-export accounting, an open dataset of stranded-clean-TWh by region, pilot policy that credits exported compute against renewable curtailment).

Match Nature Energy norms: ~3,500 words main text, ~6 display items, a structured ~150-word abstract, a Methods section that makes any quantitative estimate auditable, and 60-90 dense, fully-sourced references. Flag authorial judgement openly ('Our view is that...') rather than disguising opinion as fact — the Perspective genre rewards a clear, owned argument backed by checkable numbers.

title: Scientific discovery in the age of artificial intelligence
venue: Nature (flagship), vol. 620, pp. 47-60 (2023). Genre: Perspective (Wang, Fu, Du et al.; corresponding author Marinka Zitnik)
claimSentence: Central claim (framing thesis, not a single falsifiable proposition): "AI has emerged as a transformative technology poised to revolutionize scientific discovery"; and operationally, "AI can aid scientific discovery in two main ways. First, it can enhance existing research by accelerating pipelines or improving predictions [e.g., AlphaFold2]. Second, AI can create new tools that transform scientific research [e.g., real-time magnetic control of tokamak plasmas]." The piece organizes this into a unifying frame: a discipline-agnostic AI toolkit (self-supervised learning, geometric deep learning, generative and reinforcement-learning methods) maps onto every stage of the scientific method, so that "the development of AI algorithms cuts across traditionally isolated disciplines."

sectionFlow.heading: 1. Introduction (no subheadings; ~6 paragraphs)
sectionFlow.move: Establishes the scientific method as a universal pipeline (hypothesize -> design -> collect -> analyze), then historicizes AI as the latest in a lineage of discovery-transforming technologies (microscopes, digitization in the 1950s, data science in the 2010s). Names the enabling conditions (big data + GPUs/supercomputers + new algorithms), previews the five-method toolkit (deferring definitions to Box 1), states what makes science a uniquely hard AI domain (10^60 hypothesis space, costly labels), then asserts the two-way value thesis with two flagship anchors (AlphaFold2, tokamak control). Closes the intro with a roadmap sentence naming the article's three pillars plus grand challenges.

sectionFlow.heading: 2. AI-guided measurements and extraction of representations
sectionFlow.move: First body pillar = the DATA/INPUT stage. Two labeled sub-sections ('Facilitating scientific data collection' and 'Learning compact representations of scientific data') each broken into named micro-moves (Data selection / annotation / synthetic generation / refinement; then Geometric priors / Self-supervised learning / Language modeling / Transformers / Neural operators). Each micro-move = one sub-claim defended by 1-3 cross-disciplinary examples. Advances the argument that AI solves the input bottleneck across physics, biology, Earth science.

sectionFlow.heading: 3. AI-based generation of scientific hypotheses
sectionFlow.move: Second pillar = the HYPOTHESIS stage. Organized by three complementary technical strategies as headings: 'Black-box predictors of hypotheses' (screening/prioritization), 'Navigating combinatorial spaces of possible hypotheses' (reinforcement learning over discrete search), and 'Optimizing differentiable space to extract scientific hypotheses' (VAE latent-space + gradient methods). Each subsection states the method's strength and explicitly names its limitation (e.g., black boxes need huge data and lack interpretability; RL gets stuck in local optima; latent-space extrapolation is limited).

sectionFlow.heading: 4. AI-assisted experimentation and simulation
sectionFlow.move: Third pillar = the EXPERIMENT/VALIDATION stage. Splits into 'Efficient evaluation of scientific hypotheses' (sub-moves: Planning experiments, Steering experiments) and 'Deducing observables from hypotheses with simulations' (sub-moves: Fitting parameters, Solving differential equations, Statistical modeling of states). Carries the worked tokamak and molecular-dynamics cases. Completes the scientific-loop coverage so the reader sees AI threaded through every stage.

sectionFlow.heading: 5. Grand challenges
sectionFlow.move: The combined counterargument + limits + outlook section, deliberately the longest non-technical block. Three sub-blocks: 'Practical considerations' (open data, robotics/self-driving labs, implementation/reproducibility/transparency), 'Advancing AI algorithms' (causality & OOD generalization, multimodal learning, knowledge-grounded models, model understanding/black boxes), and 'Scientific enterprise' (conduct of science, workforce stewardship/education, misuse). Each names specific deficits rather than vague gaps.

sectionFlow.heading: Conclusion (no subheading)
sectionFlow.move: Single tight paragraph: restates the framing (build models from data, alone or with simulation/compute), re-balances promise against safety/security risk, and converts the claim into normative future directions (reliable cross-field frameworks, embedding domain knowledge, quantifying uncertainty/error/utility, responsible implementation).

openingMove: Opens not with a startling statistic but with a calm, universal premise every scientist accepts: "Throughout various stages of any research project, scientists formulate hypotheses, design simulations and experiments, and collect data to analyze and understand a natural phenomenon." It then earns timeliness through a compressed historical arc - microscopes/bootstrapping, 1950s digitization, 2010s rise of deep learning and data science - culminating in "The rise of deep learning in the early 2010s has had a significant impact on scientific research, bringing about a paradigm shift." The hook works by analogy and inevitability: AI is positioned as the next instrument in a centuries-long lineage, so the reader accepts the premise before any specific claim is argued. The "why now" is pinned to concrete recent enablers (large datasets + GPUs/supercomputers + new algorithms) and two 2021-2022 landmark results (AlphaFold2 solving the 50-year protein-folding problem; tokamak plasma control).
evidenceUse: Evidence is marshalled as a dense lattice of representative published exemplars rather than original data - the authority comes from breadth across disciplines (physics, chemistry, biology, astronomy, Earth science, mathematics) plus a handful of memorable quantitative anchors. Recurring numerical hooks: ~10^60 drug-like molecules vs <10^10 in the largest libraries (used twice, in intro and the differentiable-space section, to dramatize hypothesis-space vastness); a particle collision experiment generating >100 TB/second with >99.99% background discarded; <1% of sequenced proteins reliably annotated; 1.6 million OLED candidates and 11 billion synthon-based ligands screened; AlphaFold2 'near-experimental accuracy'; a VAE method 'up to six orders of magnitude faster'; 158 existing + 351 proposed Amazon dams. Numbers are deployed to size a problem or quantify a speedup, each tied to a citation. With 236 references, almost every clause carries a bracketed citation; flagship results (AlphaFold2, tokamak, mathematical-conjecture refutation) are reused as load-bearing case studies across multiple sections.
counterargumentHandling: Objections are engaged in two ways. Locally and continuously: nearly every technical subsection ends by naming the method's failure mode in the field's own terms - black-box predictors "require large training datasets and offer limited interpretability"; reinforcement learning "may not generalize well... the agent may get stuck in a local optimum"; latent-space optimization has limited "extrapolation ability to sparsely explored regions"; transformers "scale quadratically." Globally: the dedicated "Grand challenges" section is the article's honest counterargument block, confronting data quality/stewardship, reproducibility ("AI approaches can suffer from reproducibility due to the stochastic nature of model training"), the causality/OOD-generalization gap (conceding "human brains can better and faster generalize"), opacity of black boxes in high-stakes domains, energy/compute cost, and outright misuse/dual-use and security risk. The abstract itself foregrounds the counterargument: "central issues remain, such as understanding when AI is not helpful, counterproductive, or in need of improvement." This balance is what keeps it scholarship rather than advocacy.
closingMove: Closes with a short Conclusion that restates the unifying frame (AI = building models from data, used alone or with simulation and scalable computing) and immediately re-weighs it against risk ("it also raises concerns regarding safety and security"). It then translates the thesis into four concrete, non-generic future directions: developing reliable frameworks adaptable across fields; incorporating domain knowledge into AI systems; quantifying uncertainty, error, and utility; and prioritizing responsible implementation "to minimize risks and maximize benefits." The longer, more specific forward-looking content actually lives in the preceding 'Grand challenges' section, so the Conclusion functions as a compact moral/strategic coda rather than the sole outlook.
figureUse: Four conceptual figures plus one glossary box - no raw data plots; every figure carries one restatable message about the ARGUMENT, not about a dataset. Fig 1 ('The use of AI in science') is the master schematic: a circular wheel of interconnected discovery stages with representative studies as bullets, visually encoding the central thesis that one AI toolkit spans all stages and disciplines. Fig 2 ('Strategies of learning meaningful scientific representations') is a three-panel method primer (a geometric priors/invariance-equivariance, b self-supervised contrastive learning, c masked language modeling) mapping one panel per representation sub-claim. Fig 3 ('AI strategies for generating scientific hypotheses') mirrors Section 3's three subsections (a black-box screening, b RL navigator/parse-tree, c VAE differentiator/latent landscape) - figure structure is isomorphic to section structure. Fig 4 ('Scenarios on how AI facilitates simulations and experiments') shows three worked cases (a tokamak RL control loop, b uncertainty-guided molecular dynamics, c physics-informed neural PDE solver). Box 1 is a 20-term glossary that offloads all method definitions so the body prose stays argument-focused. Design lesson: figures are one-per-pillar and panel-per-subclaim, making the visual layout a map of the text's logic.
lengthRefsApprox: Approx. 7,500-8,000 words of main text (published over Nature pp. 47-60, ~14 journal pages - long for a Perspective, near Review length, which the flagship permits for major surveys). 236 numbered references (far above the typical 30-100 Perspective range; functions partly as a field map) plus a curated "Highlighted references" list of ~30 annotated key papers. Display items: 4 conceptual figures + 1 glossary box (Box 1) = 5 display items, at the top of the typical 2-5 range. Abstract ~150 words, unstructured, no citations or figure calls. Note: the source analyzed is the author's accepted manuscript on MIT DSpace (carries an internal '[M:]' editorial note and OCR-garbled figure-caption art); section flow, arguments, figures, box, and references match the published version.
transferableLessons: Anchor timeliness in a lineage, then a crossover. This paper earns 'why now' by placing AI in a centuries-long instrument lineage (microscope -> digitization -> data science -> deep learning). For the stranded-clean-electricity Perspective, open the same way: site the argument in the lineage of moving energy as a higher-value carrier (coal-by-rail -> gas-by-LNG -> electrons-by-HVDC -> compute-by-fiber), then pin 'now' to a concrete recent cost/efficiency crossover (e.g., GPU $/token falling, datacenter PUE, curtailment hours rising, an HVDC-vs-fiber cost figure for a specific stranded resource).

Make the central claim a frame that organizes everything, and state it as a two-way value proposition. Here the thesis ('AI spans every stage of discovery') and the operational claim ('AI either accelerates existing pipelines OR creates new tools') govern section order. Mirror this: thesis = 'export tokens, not electrons'; operationalize as (i) it monetizes electricity that would otherwise be curtailed/stranded, and (ii) it sidesteps the transmission-buildout bottleneck entirely. Pin a one-sentence version above your draft and test every paragraph against it.

Build sections as an end-to-end pipeline, not a topic list. The body walks the scientific method stage-by-stage (data -> hypothesis -> experiment). Structure yours as the energy-export value chain: stranded generation -> on-site conversion to compute -> token output -> delivery/market -> grid/policy implications. Argument-ordered, not topic-ordered.

One conceptual figure per pillar, one panel per sub-claim, and a master schematic up front. Fig 1 is a wheel encoding the whole thesis; Figs 2-4 are panel-isomorphic to their sections. Plan: a master 'electrons vs tokens' before/after schematic; a back-of-envelope cost-crossover figure ($/MWh exported as electrons via HVDC vs $/MWh embodied in tokens via datacenter+fiber); a map/scenario fan of stranded resources; a decision tree for when token-export beats electron-export. Each figure must carry a single restatable message.

Use a few memorable quantitative anchors and reuse them. The 10^60-vs-10^10 molecule figure recurs to dramatize scale. Pick 2-3 signature numbers (e.g., $/MWh delivered as electrons over X km vs embodied in compute; TWh/yr of curtailed renewables; fiber bandwidth cost per useful FLOP) and let them recur as the spine. Present every number as a sourced range, never a bare figure.

Concede limitations inside each section, not only at the end. Every technical subsection here names its own failure mode. Do the same: latency/locality (some compute must be near users), water and land for datacenters, hardware-embodied carbon, demand-shape mismatch with intermittent supply, jurisdictional/data-sovereignty constraints. Naming these in-line is what converts advocacy into credible scholarship.

Add a dedicated 'Grand challenges'-style section as your honest counterargument block. Reserve a clearly headed section for the strongest objections (Why not just build transmission? Why not batteries/hydrogen/synthetic fuels? Is AI demand durable or a bubble? Grid-reliability and curtailment-accounting subtleties) and rebut each in its strongest form before answering.

Offload definitions to a glossary box and keep body prose argument-only. Box 1 lets the body stay claim-focused. Put curtailment, LCOE, PUE, stranded vs constrained generation, token, HVDC, and embodied-carbon definitions in a box so the main text never stalls to define terms.

Use a curated 'highlighted/key references' list to signal command of the field without bloating prose. Even with a normal reference count, an annotated shortlist of the 5-8 load-bearing studies (a curtailment dataset, an HVDC cost study, a datacenter-siting-near-renewables case, a token-economics analysis) builds authority cheaply.

Close with specific, assignable next steps, not 'more research is needed.' The conclusion converts the thesis into named directions and actors. End yours with falsifiable, owned actions: a metric (levelized cost per delivered useful-token vs per delivered MWh), who should build the first co-located pilot, what policy/accounting change (counting exported compute toward renewable-utilization targets) would unlock it, and the threshold conditions under which token-export dominates electron-export.

title: Deep learning and process understanding for data-driven Earth system science
venue: Nature (flagship), 2019, vol. 566, pp. 195-204 (Perspective). Authors: Reichstein, Camps-Valls, Stevens, Jung, Denzler, Carvalhais, Prabhat.
claimSentence: Central thesis (stated in the summary paragraph and reasserted in the conclusion): rather than amending classical machine learning, contextual spatio-temporal cues "should be at the core of a modified approach -- termed deep learning -- to extract novel understanding and predictive ability," and "a critical further step will be a hybrid modeling approach coupling physical processes with deep learning versatility." Restated in the conclusion as: "future models should integrate process-based and machine learning approaches. Data-driven machine learning approaches to geo-scientific research will not replace physical modelling, but strongly complement and enrich it... with the ultimate goal of hybrid modelling approaches."

sectionFlow.heading: Summary paragraph (unnumbered abstract)
sectionFlow.move: Compresses the entire argument into 6 sentences: states the problem (ML used on exploding geodata but suboptimal when behaviour is context-dominated), names the proposed solution (deep learning as the core, not an add-on), and previews the forward bet (hybrid physics+DL modelling). Functions as a thesis-in-miniature.

sectionFlow.heading: 1. Introduction
sectionFlow.move: Builds the case in three beats: (a) zooms out to humanity's millennia-long quest to predict, narrowing to the weather-prediction success story and then to its limits (no skill beyond days, biosphere unpredictable); (b) establishes timeliness with the 'data deluge' (the four V's of Big Data); (c) names the gap (data collection outpaces assimilation/understanding) and frames the paper as 'two major tasks': extract knowledge from the deluge, and build models that learn from data while respecting nature's laws. Ends with an explicit roadmap sentence.

sectionFlow.heading: 2. State-of-the-art in geoscientific machine learning
sectionFlow.move: Establishes credibility and the baseline: surveys 30 years of ML success across atmosphere/land/ocean (classification, change detection, regression, flux mapping). Then pivots with 'Notwithstanding the success...' to enumerate limitations -- pitfalls (naive extrapolation, p-fishing) and, more fundamentally, the failure of classical ML to exhaustively exploit spatio-temporal context. Uses fire and hurricane examples to make the abstract limitation concrete, setting up the need for deep learning.

sectionFlow.heading: 3. Deep-learning opportunities in Earth system science
sectionFlow.move: Makes the affirmative case: shows DL's documented wins in vision/speech/physics/chemistry/biology, then argues by ANALOGY that geoscientific data structurally resemble images/video/speech (2D fields ~ RGB; time-evolving fields ~ video; geo time-series ~ speech). This analogy is the rhetorical engine -- it licenses importing DL wholesale. Cites concrete early geoscience DL successes (hurricane detection, >95% urban classification).

sectionFlow.heading: 4. Deep-learning challenges in Earth system science
sectionFlow.move: Pre-empts objections by honestly cataloguing where the analogy breaks (hundreds of spectral channels vs 3 RGB; violated i.i.d. assumption; multi-sensor fusion; petabyte/day volume; 40000x20000 vs 512x512 images; no ImageNet-style labels; 'it's a cat' vs 'it's a drought' labelling problem; underconstrained/extrapolation). Crystallizes these into an enumerated list of FIVE challenges (interpretability, physical consistency, complex/uncertain data, limited labels, computational demand). Then turns the challenges into an opportunity, arguing DL could matter MORE in geoscience than in vision precisely because hand-crafted features are missing -- 'these assumptions... are exactly the models we are looking for!'

sectionFlow.heading: 5. Integration with physical modelling
sectionFlow.move: The intellectual core and the paper's original contribution. Reframes the theory-driven vs data-driven 'two worlds' as complementary, then offers a structured taxonomy of FIVE synergy points keyed to a figure: (1) improving parameterizations, (2) replacing a sub-model with ML (the hybrid model), (3) analysing model-observation mismatch, (4) constraining sub-models, (5) surrogate modelling/emulation. Each gets a worked geoscience example. Then adds the reverse direction (encoding physics into ML via architecture, cost-function constraints, physics-based data augmentation) and names enabling methods (probabilistic and differentiable programming).

sectionFlow.heading: 6. Advancing science
sectionFlow.move: Answers the 'so what for understanding, not just prediction?' question. Argues observations have always driven scientific revolutions (Copernicus), and that data-driven ML now accelerates hypothesis generation/testing by 'orders of magnitude.' Grounded in real discoveries: ML flux estimates exposed climate-model overestimation of tropical photosynthesis and explained the high-latitude CO2 seasonal-amplitude conundrum. Defends against the 'black box can't yield understanding' critique.

sectionFlow.heading: 7. Conclusion
sectionFlow.move: Restates the thesis and converts it into FOUR concrete recommendations (recognize data particularities; ensure plausibility/interpretability; estimate uncertainty; test against complex physical models). Closes on the hybrid-modelling vision and names two grand challenges (atmospheric convection parameterization; spatio-temporal ecosystem dependence) that the approach could finally crack.

openingMove: Opens with a wide-angle, almost philosophical hook: "Humans have always been striving to predict and understand the world," sweeping from ancient Greek reasoning through medieval soothsaying to modern hypothesis-testing and computer modelling. It immediately funnels to a concrete success story (weather prediction) and its hard limit ("we can only accurately predict the evolution of the weather on a time-scale of days, not months"). Timeliness is then manufactured in the very next paragraph by the 'data deluge': storage already beyond dozens of petabytes, transmission beyond hundreds of terabytes/day, CMIP-5 at 3PB heading to CMIP-6 at 30PB, and the 'four V's of Big Data.' The hook pairs an ancient human aspiration with a brand-new, quantified resource (data) to create urgency.
evidenceUse: Evidence is marshalled as a dense citation carpet (102 references) of prior published work rather than new experiments -- appropriate for a Perspective. Numbers are used selectively for scale and credibility: petabyte/terabyte data volumes, '15 or more orders of temporal and spatial magnitude,' CMIP 3PB-to-30PB, '>95%' urban classification accuracy, '512x512 vs 40000x20000 pixels (three orders of magnitude),' 32/64-bit precision, nowcasting 'up to two hours,' LSTM with 8 cells trained on 80% of data (supplementary). Qualitative evidence dominates the argument: named, concrete case studies (eddy-covariance CO2 flux ANN, global photosynthesis/ET mapping, ocean carbon neural nets, hydrological parameter regionalization, convection parameterization, sea-surface-temperature hybrid model). Each abstract claim is anchored to a specific cited example, and several 'firsts' are flagged in annotated references.
counterargumentHandling: Counterarguments are engaged head-on and constructively, not dismissed. Section 2 concedes ML's pitfalls (naive extrapolation, sampling bias, confounders, mistaking correlation for causation, p-fishing) before advancing. Section 4 is essentially one long good-faith concession: it lists every way geoscience data DIFFER from the vision/speech data DL was built for, then converts the deficit into the central opportunity ('these assumptions... are exactly the models we are looking for'). Section 6 directly rebuts the strongest objection to the thesis -- that opaque statistical models cannot advance understanding -- by arguing (with examples) that ML accelerates the classic hypothesis-generation/testing loop and even notes that complex physical Earth-system models are themselves 'often not easily traceable.' The interpretability and physical-consistency worries are repeatedly acknowledged and folded into the recommendations rather than waved away.
closingMove: Closes by restating the thesis as a settled stance ('will not replace physical modelling, but strongly complement and enrich it') and crystallizing it into four prescriptive, reusable recommendations. The final paragraph paints the aspirational end-state -- hybrid models that 'obey physical laws, feature a conceptualized and thus interpretable structure, and at the same time are fully data-adaptive where theory is weak' -- and explicitly notes the bidirectionality (ML also benefits from physics). It ends with a forward-looking flourish naming two long-standing 'resistant' grand challenges (convection parameterization; spatio-temporal ecosystem-climate dependence) now 'open to be addressed,' leaving the reader with concrete targets rather than vague optimism.
figureUse: Figures are conceptual/schematic, not data plots -- standard for a Perspective. Figure 1 visualizes the abstract 'four V's of Big Data' challenge in a geoscience frame (orienting/motivational). Figure 2 is the load-bearing rhetorical device: a two-column layout pairing canonical DL applications (left) with the analogous geoscience problem (right), literally drawing the analogy that the whole argument rests on. Figure 3 is the taxonomy figure -- an abstracted physical model whose submodels carry numbered black-boxes (1-5) that the Section 5 prose maps onto one-to-one ('the numbers in the following list correspond to the circles in the figure'). Figure 4 illustrates the headline 'hybrid model' idea as 'physicizing' a neural net by stacking physical layers on top, with two concrete instantiations (B, C). A Table (Table 1) compactly cross-tabulates analytical task / conventional approach / limitation / emergent DL approach -- a scannable evidence summary. Supplementary figures + a worked synthetic dynamical-system box (logistic-map example, LSTM vs RF/ANN) provide the technical proof-of-concept kept out of the main flow.
lengthRefsApprox: Main text approximately 5,500-6,000 words (full author postprint including supplementary ~11,900 words). References: 102. Display items: 4 main figures + 1 table in the main article; plus 3 supplementary figures, 1 supplementary worked-example box, and a ~14-term glossary. Structure: unnumbered summary paragraph + 7 numbered sections.
transferableLessons: Front-load a thesis-in-miniature: write a 5-6 sentence summary that states problem, names your reframe, and previews the forward bet. For the AI-compute Perspective: 'Stranded clean electricity is wasted as electrons; we argue it should be exported as tokens -- AI compute -- because compute is locationally fungible in a way kWh are not, and a colocated-compute build-out is the missing-money fix for curtailment.' Then echo this verbatim in the conclusion.

Open with a wide aspiration + a sharp, quantified limit. Reichstein pairs 'humans always wanted to predict' with 'but only days, not months.' Analogue: pair 'the world is racing to decarbonize the grid' with a hard number on curtailed/stranded renewable energy (TWh/yr curtailed, negative-price hours, transmission queue backlog) to manufacture timeliness.

Manufacture urgency with a 'deluge' of quantified trend lines. They used PB/TB data volumes and CMIP 3PB->30PB. You should use the analogous scaling pair: surging stranded-renewable capacity AND surging datacenter/AI electricity demand and token throughput -- two exponentials whose intersection is your whole argument.

Build your case via a structural ANALOGY, then make a figure carry it. Their Figure 2 literally pairs DL-application with geoscience-problem. Build the equivalent two-column figure: 'electron export (HVDC, H2, ammonia)' vs 'token export (fiber + colocated compute)', mapping transmission losses/lead-times/fungibility side by side. The figure should do argumentative work, not decorate.

Earn the right to your claim by surveying the state of the art first (Section 2 pattern), citing real deployments (existing colocated datacenters at stranded hydro/solar/flared-gas sites, grid-aware compute scheduling). Establish you know the baseline before proposing the reframe.

Dedicate a whole section to honestly cataloguing where your analogy BREAKS, then convert the deficit into opportunity (their Section 4 'these assumptions are exactly the models we are looking for'). For tokens-not-electrons: latency, data sovereignty, water/cooling, capex stranding if renewables move, demand-response inflexibility -- list them, then argue why colocated compute is uniquely suited (interruptible, latency-tolerant batch/training loads).

Offer a numbered TAXONOMY keyed to a figure (their five synergy points = Figure 3). Give the reader a clean enumerated menu, e.g. five modes of 'compute as energy export': (1) training/batch inference colocation, (2) curtailment-absorbing flexible load, (3) firming via compute load-shedding, (4) value-add vs raw export, (5) avoided transmission capex. One worked real-world example per item.

Pre-empt the killer objection in its own section (their Section 6 rebuts 'black boxes can't yield understanding'). Yours must rebut 'this is just speculative load-shifting / jevons paradox / it strands assets.' Use real numbers and concede where physical export (interconnects) still wins.

Close with concrete, prescriptive recommendations, not vague optimism (their four recommendations). E.g. siting/permitting reforms, market design for interruptible compute, carbon-accounting standards for token-embodied energy, metrics (tokens/MWh, gCO2/token). End by naming 1-2 grand challenges your approach uniquely unlocks (e.g. monetizing otherwise-curtailed remote renewables; decoupling load growth from transmission build-out).

Match the genre's quantitative texture: ~5,000-6,000 words, ~80-110 references dominated by recent primary literature and a few flagged 'firsts,' 3-5 conceptual (not data) display items, an unnumbered lead summary, and section headings that are claims/themes rather than generic labels. Hedge appropriately ('we argue,' 'most promising,' 'envision') while keeping the spine assertive.

Use scale-numbers for credibility but let named case studies carry persuasion. They never over-quantified the argument; every abstract point landed on a concrete cited example. Anchor each of your modes to a real site/deployment so the Perspective reads as grounded extrapolation, not manifesto.
